title: Research
text:
PhD Research
Thesis: “An Evaluation of Multi-Agency Front Door Services in England” (UCL Social Research Institute, 2026)
Supervised by Professor Lorraine Dearden, Professor Katie Harron and Professor Jenny Woodman. ESRC UBEL Doctoral Training Partnership studentship, co-funded by Foundations.
My doctoral research examined the implementation and effectiveness of Multi-Agency Front Door Services (MAFDs) across England using:

ECHILD: Linked administrative data from the Children in Need census, National Pupil Database and Hospital Episode Statistics (2008 to 2022), covering about 2.7 million first referrals to children’s social care
National survey: Designed and fielded in REDCap to all 152 English local authorities, with a 73% response rate (111 of 152)
Text mining: Web scraped and analysed 3,000+ Ofsted reports to date the implementation of MAFDs in each local authority
Quasi-experimental methods: Difference-in-differences under staggered adoption, event studies and synthetic controls

title: Dr Rocío (Ro) Méndez Pineda
text:
I am a Research Fellow in Epidemiology and Statistics at UCL Great Ormond Street Institute of Child Health, working in Population Health Improvement UK and the NIHR Children and Families Policy Research Unit. I use national linked administrative data, ECHILD, to understand inequalities in young people’s access to mental health services.
I completed my PhD at the UCL Social Research Institute in 2026. It evaluated Multi-Agency Safeguarding Hubs and other multi-agency front door services in children’s social care across England. I was research lead on the Evaluation of Multi-Agency Safeguarding Hubs, commissioned by the Department for Education. It contributed evidence to the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026 and was cited in the Sara Sharif Child Safeguarding Practice Review.
I have taught quantitative methods at UCL since 2022 and teach on the Introduction to ECHILD course for researchers using linked data. Before moving into child health and social care, I worked on the measurement of job quality in Latin America and the EU.

title: Research
text:
Current Work
Inequalities in referrals to NHS mental health services. A two-paper programme applying intersectional MAIHDA (multilevel analysis of individual heterogeneity and discriminatory accuracy) to referrals of school pupils in England, using the National Pupil Database linked to the Mental Health Services Data Set in ECHILD. This is part of the Population Mental Health Consortium (Population Health Improvement UK), where I am research lead for the challenge area on children and young people’s mental health. The analysis compares referral across groups defined by ethnicity, gender, free school meal eligibility and English as an additional language. Workshops with young people, facilitated by Leaders Unlocked, showed that where they live matters to them, so the analysis now includes an urban and rural dimension. We plan to write part of the first paper with young people from the workshops, so that their perspective appears in their own words.
Relationships and Sex Education and young people’s mental health. A quasi-experimental evaluation of statutory Relationships and Sex Education and mental health inequality between sexual minority and heterosexual adolescents, using the UK Household Longitudinal Study. Paper in preparation.
Multi-agency front doors in children’s social care. Two papers from my PhD are in preparation: the quasi-experimental evaluation, and a method for dating policy implementation by text mining Ofsted reports.

title: Research
text:
Earlier Work
Before my PhD I worked on the multidimensional measurement of job quality and regional inequality in Latin America, Egypt and the EU, at the LSE International Inequalities Institute and Universidad de Chile. That work still shapes how I think about measurement and cross-national comparison.
